title: 11.1 Coulomb's law — Introduction
paragraphs: Electrostatics is the studies of electric charges which are at rest or static. The electric force between static charged particles is known as the electrostatic force.

The electrostatic force is attractive or repulsive force between particles that are caused due to their electric charges. It is also referred to as Coulomb's force. In SI units, charge is measured in coulombs (symbol C). The charge q is quantized and it is an integral multiple of elementary charge e, i.e., \(q=ne\).
Another quantity being discussed that plays an important role in electrical circuits is capacitance and its dependence on the dielectrics.
11.1 COULOMB'S LAW

The quantitative measurement of the force between two electric charges was first made by Coulomb. He carried out series of experiments to measure the force between electric charges using an apparatus known as torsion balance. Coulomb expresses his experimental data in the form of a statement which is known as Coulomb's law.

It states “the magnitude of the force between two point charges, is directly proportional to the product of the magnitudes of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.”
Charles-Augustin de Coulom was an eminent Frenc physicist who formulated th law known Coulomb's law

title: Coulomb’s law in material media
paragraphs: The constant k can be generally expressed in terms of permittivity of the free space \(\varepsilon_0\) i.e., \(k=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\)
Experimentally measured value of \(\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\;\mathrm{C^2\,N^{-1}\,m^{-2}}\)
so \(k=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=9.0\times10^9\;\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}\)
COULOMB’S LAW IN MATERIAL MEDIA

Eq:(11.2) gives the force between two charges when there is air or vacuum between them. But it is experimentally observed that when an insulator is placed between the electric charges, it reduces the force. Permittivity is the property of a medium which affects the magnitude of force between two point charges.
The coulomb’s force can now be written as
\(F_{\mathrm{med}}=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon}\frac{q_1q_2}{r^2}\) … (11.5)

The quantity \(\varepsilon\) is called the permittivity of the medium. For a particular insulator the permittivity of a material medium compared with the permittivity of vacuum is called relative permittivity or dielectric constant \(\varepsilon_r\). Its ratio is given by
\(\varepsilon_r=\frac{\varepsilon}{\varepsilon_0}\) … (11.6)

title: Example 11.1 — Solution
paragraphs: Electrostatic force on charge \(q_2\) due to charge \(q_1\)= \(F_{21}=k\frac{q_1q_2}{r_{12}^2}\)
\(=9.0\times10^9\;\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}\frac{(5\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm C)(10\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm C)}{(6\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m)^2}\)
Electrostatic force on charge \(q_2\) due to \(q_3\)=
\(F_{23}=9.0\times10^9\;\mathrm{N\,m^2\,C^{-2}}\frac{(10\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm C)(12\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm C)}{4\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm m}\)
\(=\frac{1080\times10^{-3}}{16\times10^{-4}}\,\mathrm N=675\,\mathrm N\)
The net electrostatic force on charge \(q_2=F_2=F_{21}-F_{23}\)
\(=675\,\mathrm N-125\,\mathrm N=550\,\mathrm N\).
The direction of the net electrostatic force on charge \(q_2\) points towards charge \(q_3\) (points to the right).

title: 11.2 Electric field and its intensity
paragraphs: The concept of electric field was first proposed by Michael Faraday, in the 19th century. He stated that the electric field around a charge is like a sphere with in which other charges are influenced by it.
An electric field is defined as any region around a charge in which an electric test charge would experience an electric force.

Electric field is characterized by strength and direction at every point in space. The strength and direction of electric field can be determined by placing a unit positive test charge in that field. The direction in which this unit positive test charge move or tends to move is the direction of electric field. The test charge is so small that it does not distort the original field due to the primary source.

A single vector quantity containing information about the field strength and its direction at that point is denoted by \(\vec E\) and is known as electric field intensity. If unit positive test charge \(q_0\) experience a force \(F\) due to the electric field of charge q. Then
the intensity of an electric field at any point is the force per unit positive test charge placed at that point.
The electric field intensity \(\vec E=\frac{\vec F}{q_0}\)
Or \(\vec F=q_0\vec E\) … (11.9)

title: Electric field intensity due to a point charge
paragraphs: The SI unit of electric field intensity is newton per coulomb \((\mathrm{N\,C^{-1}})\) or volt per metre \((\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})\).
Coulomb’s law enables the electric field to be calculated for any point in space around a fixed static charge q. The magnitude of electric field is given by:
As \(\hat r\) is the unit vector directed from charge q to \(q_0\) so in vector form
\(\vec F=\frac{kqq_0}{r^2}\hat r\)
So the field intensity is given by
\(\vec E=\frac{\vec F}{q_0}=k\frac{qq_0/r^2}{q_0}\hat r\)
\(\vec E=k\frac{q}{r^2}\hat r\) … (11.10)
The strength of the field is proportional to the magnitude of the charge. Its strength decreases as the test charge moves away (unit charge) from source charge q.

title: 11.2.1 Representation of electric field by lines
paragraphs: In the previous section, the vector nature of the electric field strength was discussed. An electric field can be used in the pictorial form to describe the overall intensity of the field around it. This pictorial representation is called the electric field lines.
An electric field line is an imaginary line or curve drawn through a region of empty space. The direction of the electric field at point A, B, C and D is tangent to the field line through that point.

The electric field lines, point in the direction that a positive test charge would accelerate if placed upon the line. The arrows indicate the electric field at different points. The direction of these arrows is outward for positive charge and is inward for negative charge as shown in Fig: 11.4.
The field lines starts from positive charge and terminate at negative charge as shown in Fig: (11.5)

Fig: 11.6 show two infinitely large parallel plates separated by a very small distance. The upper plate has a uniform positive charge distribution while the lower plate has a negative one. If the plates are not of infinite length, the field lines at the ends of plates will be a little bulging out, showing that field is not uniform at the ends. The field such as at the ends of plates is called “fringing field”.

Another interesting property of field lines can be explained with the help of Fig. 11.7. Suppose that a charge +q is placed near a metal plate. The positive charge will attract the negative charges (electrons) in the metal plate, resulting in the motion of these charges until some of them reach that surface of the metal which is near to +q charge where they will be at rest. The electric lines of force cannot pass through a conductor. Therefore electric field is zero inside a conductor.

title: 11.4 ELECTRIC FLUX
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: The concept of flux describes how much of something goes through a given area. You may conceptualize the flux of an electric field as a measure of the number of electric field lines passing through an area. For discussing the flux of a vector field, it is helpful to introduce an area vector \(\vec A\). The area vector of a flat surface has magnitude equal to area (A) and its direction is along the normal to the surface \((\hat n)\) as shown in figure 11.11.

The electric flux is denoted by \(\Phi_E\). For uniform field \(\vec E\) and area \(\vec A\) electric flux is defined as the measure of number of lines of force that pass through the area placed in the electric field. Flux \(\Phi_E\) is the scalar product of the electric field E and plane surface area A.
\(\Phi_E=\vec E\cdot\vec A\)
The electric flux \(\Phi_E\) depends upon:
i. surface area
ii. electric field intensity
iii. the orientation of surface area A with respect to the field lines E.
FLUX AT ANY ANGLE (θ) :
if the area \(\vec A\) is tilted such that it is making an angle θ with the electric field lines as shown in figure(11.11 b) in this case the electric flux is
\(\Phi_E=\vec E\cdot\vec A=EA\cos\theta\)
The number of lines passing through the area will be E (A cosθ) depending upon angle θ.
MAXIMUM FLUX:

if the surface is placed perpendicular to the electric field such that surface area \(\vec A\) is parallel to electric field \(\vec E\) then maximum electric lines of force will pass through the surface as shown in figure 11.11c.

title: Electric flux (continued)
sourcePdf: Books/12th/12th Physics/PDF/Physics Book for 12 class KPTBB.pdf
paragraphs: Consequently maximum electric lines will pass through the surface.
The electric flux is \(\Phi_E=EA\cos0=EA\)
Therefore large number of lines passes through the area.
ZERO FLUX:

if the surface is placed parallel to the electric field such that surface area \(\vec A\) is normal to electric field \(\vec E\) then no electric lines of force will pass through the surface as shown in Figure 11.11d. Consequently no electric flux will pass through the surface.
Then flux is \(\Phi_E=EA\cos90=0\)
ELECTRIC FLUX THROUGH CLOSE SURFACE

If the case is such that either field is non-uniform or the surface is curved, then we divide the surfaces into very small patches of area \(\Delta A\) called differential area and assume that these are approximately flat and they are so small that electric field \(E\) is almost uniform over it. For one of these small patches of area as shown in Fig.11.12 . The electric flux is defined by the relation. (Differential form),
\(\Phi_E=E\cdot\Delta A\)
To calculate total flux through the whole surface we add flux from each patch such that
\(\Phi_E=\sum\vec E\cdot\Delta\vec A\)

In case of closed surface the electric flux may be positive negative or zero depending upon the number of lines entering or leaving the surface:
(i) The electric flux is zero if numbers of field lines entering are equal to field line leaving the surface or no field line intercepting the surface as shown in fig (a).
(ii) The electric flux is negative if net numbers of electric field lines are entering the closed surface or more field lines are entering than leaving the surface as shown in fig (b).

paragraphs: The electric flux through the small elements \(\Delta A_1\) is
\(\Phi_1=\vec E_1\cdot\Delta\vec A_1=E_1\Delta A_1\cos0=E_1\Delta A_1\)
The electric flux through the other small element \(\Delta A_2\) is

title: Gauss’s law — total enclosed charge

paragraphs: \(\Phi_E=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_o}\frac1{r^2}(4\pi r^2)\)

The above equation shows that electric flux does not depend upon the shape or geometry of a closed surface. But it depends upon the medium and the charge enclosed by that surface.

In order to calculate the electric flux through irregular close surface S, enclosing point charges \(q_1,q_2,q_3,\ldots,q_n\) as shown in Fig 11.15 a. Then the total electric flux through that closed surface is
\(\Phi_E=\frac{q_1}{\varepsilon_o}+\frac{q_2}{\varepsilon_o}+\frac{q_3}{\varepsilon_o}\ldots\frac{q_n}{\varepsilon_o}\)
\(=\frac1{\varepsilon_o}(q_1+q_2+q_3+\ldots q_n)\)
\(\Phi_E=\frac1{\varepsilon_o}\sum_{i=1}^{n}q_i\)
\(=\frac1{\varepsilon_o}\) (total charge enclosed by a surface)
\(=\frac Q{\varepsilon_o}\)
Thus Gauss’s law shows that the electric flux through any closed surface is \(1/\varepsilon_o\) times the total charge enclosed in it.
